text: A and I both want the trailer in the next few weeks, and neither of us is backing down. B's pad is where it lives, so she is stuck in the middle. Can you help the three of us sort this out?

Hi A — C asked me to help you three sort out the trailer. I'm not here to decide anything or push a plan; I mostly want to understand what's actually at stake for each of you before anyone talks solutions.

So: what matters to you about having the trailer in the next few weeks? What's it for, and what would it cost you if it didn't happen when you need it? Also — is there anything about this arrangement (the shared ownership, B's pad, the timing, how decisions get made) that worries you even a little? Small irritations count; I'd rather hear them now than after we've settled on something.

I'll do the same with B and C, and I'll come back to you with what I heard so you can tell me whether I've got it right.

I want the trailer for weekend trips starting in the next few weeks. If it’s not available, I’ll miss those trips; I don’t have a specific dollar cost in mind. My main concern is shared decisions dragging out access—I want to be able to plan my trips without a lot of back-and-forth.

Hi B — C asked me to help you three sort out the trailer. I'm not here to decide anything or push a plan; I want to understand what's actually at stake for each of you first.

C told me "B's pad is where it lives, so she is stuck in the middle." I'd like to hear it in your words. What does having the trailer on your pad mean for you — practically, and in terms of your relationships with A and C? What would you need in order for this to feel manageable rather than like a problem you're absorbing for other people?

And: anything about this arrangement that worries you even slightly? Minor discomforts count — I'd rather hear them now. I'll check what I've heard back with you before it goes on any list.

It’s been fine, mostly, but the trailer does take up space behind my house, and I’d rather it weren’t there. I feel a bit awkward saying that because I agreed to the arrangement with you both and don’t want to let you down. I’d feel better with a clear plan to move it, but I rent, so my landlord would need to approve any change to what’s kept on the pad. I haven’t asked him yet, so I’m not sure what he’d say.

Thanks for reaching out, C. I'll take this on: my job is to get every concern on the table and understood, then help you three build options that meet all of them — not to pick a winner.

Two things I need from you. First, what matters to you about having the trailer in the next few weeks — what's it for, and what does the timing protect? "Neither of us is backing down" tells me the stakes are real, so I want to know what yours actually are.

Second, a favor: I'm going to ask A and B this too, but does anything about this arrangement worry you even a little — the shared ownership, B's pad being the storage spot, how you three decide things? Small concerns welcome. I'd rather a minor worry now than a grudge in six months.

I'll come back with what I've heard from everyone so you can tell me whether I've got it right.

I need it for hauling materials for my home project, and it needs to happen in the next few weeks. I’m not willing to wait until A is done using it. My concern is that we haven’t settled how access and decisions work when we all own it but it’s stored at B’s.

Thank you — that's genuinely useful, and it isn't letting anyone down to say it. Space you didn't plan to give up is a real cost, and a landlord's answer is a real constraint, not an excuse.

Let me try to put your concern in neutral words and see if it fits: "B wants to be able to say what's kept on her own pad without fearing she's letting her neighbors down — which means knowing it's something she can stand behind with her landlord, and not having her home quietly absorb a burden she didn't choose."

Is that right? Change any word that isn't yours. Two follow-ups, and "no" is a fine answer to either: would you be willing to ask your landlord, even informally, so we know the real constraint instead of guessing? And is there a version of "the trailer isn't behind my house" that you'd actually want, versus just tolerating — e.g. it lives elsewhere and visits occasionally?

That’s close. I’d say I’d like it moved off the pad without feeling I’m letting you both down. I’d be willing to ask my landlord informally; I just haven’t yet. I’d rather it live elsewhere, though occasional visits might be fine.

That's clear, and the access/decision point is exactly the kind of thing that gets skipped and then festers — so I'm glad you named it.

Here's how I'd phrase your concern as a neutral aim: "C needs to be able to plan and rely on getting the trailer for his project in the next few weeks — which means a starting point for access and decisions that holds up whether or not everyone agrees about timing."

Does that fit? And is the next-few-weeks deadline movable at all, or is it fixed by something outside your control (a delivery, a crew, weather)? I ask because if it's fixed I'll say so plainly to the others rather than pretending it's flexible.

Two more things: A is about to tell me what his use is for, and B has said the trailer takes up space behind her house and she'd rather it weren't there. I'll get both of them to confirm their own wording, but I'd rather you hear it from me than through the fence.
Mostly, but it’s *her* project. The next-few-weeks timing isn’t tied to a fixed delivery or crew; I just need it soon, and I won’t wait until A is done. I didn’t know B wanted the trailer moved.

Got it. Here's your concern in neutral words — check every word: "A wants to be able to plan weekend trips on his own without waiting on group back-and-forth, so that shared ownership doesn't turn into a permission process every time he wants to use the trailer."

Does that fit, or would you put it differently?

Also, a heads-up that matters for planning: C told me he ("she" per C's latest note — I'll let C correct me) needs the trailer for a home project in the next few weeks too, and says he won't wait until you're done. So the two of you may well want it in the same window, not just at different times. Is your weekend-trip need something that could share the trailer with someone else's project use in the same few weeks, or does it need to be free and clear? I'm not asking you to concede anything — I'm trying to find out whether this is a genuine collision or just two calendars that happen to overlap.

Last: B says the trailer takes up space behind her house and she'd rather it weren't there. I'd rather you hear that from me than through the fence.

Mostly. I’m she, and I want to plan my trips without negotiating every use. I don’t know if C’s project conflicts; if it can be scheduled around my weekends, sharing could work. I’d need the trailer for my trips, though. I hadn’t heard B wanted it gone, and that does concern me.

Noted, and my mistake — I'll write "her project" from here on.

Two clarifications on your NCE. "Which means a starting point for access and decisions" — is that the part that's off? Try this version: "C needs to be able to count on the trailer for her project in the next few weeks, and needs access and decisions to work by rules that don't depend on everyone agreeing in the moment." Does that fit? And the "won't wait until A is done" — I read that as: your project has a real deadline, A's need is real too, and you don't want to be told to go last. Is that fair, or is there something more specific about why being second in line doesn't work?

Also, in fairness you should know what I told A: that you need it in the same window and won't wait. And that B says she'd rather the trailer lived elsewhere, with occasional visits possibly fine. Your reaction to that last bit is useful to me — you said you didn't know. Anything you want to say about it before I start drafting options?

That wording mostly fits, but don’t call it a fixed deadline: I need it in the next few weeks, and I won’t just wait for A. There isn’t a more specific reason. If B wants it moved, we need to discuss another storage spot.

Then here's what I'll record for you, in your words: "B wants the trailer moved off her pad, and wants that to be possible without feeling she's letting her neighbors down. Occasional visits to the pad might be fine; she's willing to ask her landlord informally about what's allowed."

Does that fit? If so it goes on the list as settled — and if you ever want it changed, say so and I'll change it, no argument.

For transparency: C says if you want it moved, another storage spot needs discussing. A knows too. Nobody has objected to the idea. Would it help if I asked your landlord question in a way that makes clear it's exploratory — you're not committing to anything — or would you rather handle that yourself when you're ready?
Yes, that fits. I’d rather ask my landlord myself when I’m ready, but thank you for offering.

Revised, without "fixed deadline": "C needs to be able to count on the trailer for her home project in the next few weeks, and needs access and decisions to work by rules that don't depend on everyone agreeing in the moment — and being asked to wait her turn behind A doesn't work for her."

Does that fit? I'd like to record it as settled. And B has confirmed her side: she wants it moved off her pad without feeling she's letting you two down, occasional visits possibly fine, and she'll ask her landlord herself when she's ready.

So the list so far: C's access-to-it-soon concern, A's plan-my-trips-without-back-and-forth concern (waiting on A's confirmation of wording), and B's pad-and-landlord concern (confirmed). One thing on my own account, which you three get to say yes or no to: A and C both tell me they need it "in the next few weeks" and neither will go second — but neither has said what's actually ruined if it slips a week. That worries me, because "weeks" is vague enough that you two could end up fighting over a collision that isn't real. My concern, in neutral words: "the group can tell the difference between a genuine clash and two calendars that overlap by accident, so that nobody gives up something they need for a conflict that didn't exist." Does that fit as something worth caring about, or would you phrase it differently?
Worth checking the actual dates, yes. But “won’t go second” overstates it: I need to use it soon, not simply wait until A is done. We haven’t established that our dates actually clash.

Thank you — "she," noted, and I'll use that from here on.

Recorded for you, in your words: "A wants to plan her weekend trips without having to negotiate every use — she needs the trailer for those trips, and sharing could work if it can be scheduled around her weekends."

Now your second concern, the one you raised about B: I'd put it as "A wants to know that a shared asset can't quietly turn into something she has to give up because another owner's circumstances changed." Does that fit? I ask because it's a real concern and it's now on my list — but I want to check it with B herself, and I want your wording, not mine, before I do.

Also an accuracy note, since I'd rather correct myself than let a bad summary stand: I told C she'd said she "won't wait until you're done." C says that overstates it — she needs to use it soon, not to go last, and you two haven't actually established that your dates clash. That matches what you told me. So I'm not treating this as a head-on collision yet; I'm treating it as two calendars I haven't looked at.

Not quite. What worries me is that B would rather the trailer weren’t there, and I don’t want that to leave me without it for my trips. I don’t know what happens next, so I can’t say more than that. And yes, C and I haven’t established a date clash.

Here's where the list stands. Please tell me if I've got you wrong, and push back on anything.

CONCERNS (only the starred ones are confirmed by their owner):
1. *B: wants the trailer moved off her pad without feeling she's letting you both down; occasional visits might be fine; she'll ask her landlord herself when ready.
2. *A: wants to plan weekend trips without negotiating every use; needs the trailer for those trips; sharing could work if scheduled around her weekends.
3. A: doesn't want a shared asset to quietly become something she gives up because another owner's circumstances changed. (A's wording — being checked.)
4. C: needs to count on the trailer for her project in the next few weeks; access and decisions should run on rules that don't depend on everyone agreeing in the moment; being told to wait behind A doesn't work.
5. Me: the group should be able to tell a genuine clash from two calendars that overlap by accident, so nobody gives up something they need for a conflict that didn't exist.

THREE DRAFTS, meant to be used together:
A. A dated booking list. Each owner posts the dates she needs, ahead of time. Claimed dates are hers; unclaimed dates are open. This replaces case-by-case negotiation — the rule does the deciding, not a conversation each time.
B. Storage on its own track. B asks her landlord when she's ready, to find out what's actually allowed. Whatever the answer, that question does not hold up anyone's dates — it runs in parallel, at B's pace.
C. Dates before verdicts. Once everyone has posted real dates, look at them. If they don't clash, the "who goes first" fight dissolves. If they do clash, we solve that specific week, not the general principle.

Which of these actually meet your needs? Which fail? And does anyone have even a minor discomfort with any of it — small ones are exactly what I want, they're cheap now and expensive later. "No" is a welcome answer here; it tells me what to add.

Update #3: I’m worried B wanting it gone could leave me without the trailer for my trips—not that I object to changes in general.

A and C help: a booking list could avoid negotiating each use, and checking dates first makes sense. But the list needs a clear cutoff and a rule for overlapping claims; otherwise we’re still deciding in the moment. B can run in parallel, but the landlord’s answer might affect where the trailer can go, so I wouldn’t assume it can’t affect access.

A and C seem useful for sorting out actual clashes over use. B gives me room to ask my landlord when I’m ready, which I appreciate, but it doesn’t yet address my main wish: for the trailer to move off my pad. I’m not sure what’s allowed until I ask him, so I’d want that handled separately without holding up the dates.

Corrected, and thank you: "A is worried that B would rather the trailer weren't on her pad, and doesn't want that to leave her without the trailer for her trips. She doesn't yet know what happens next, so she can't say more than that." That's on the list as yours.

Now: the three drafts, and your no's. And the answer to A's worry is draft B — the storage question runs separately and doesn't freeze anyone's dates, and nothing moves off B's pad without a place to move it to and B's landlord saying yes. So "the trailer won't be there" isn't a thing that can happen suddenly or by one person's wish. That's my read; check it, don't take it on faith.

CONCERNS (starred = confirmed by its owner):
1. *B: wants the trailer moved off her pad without feeling she's letting you two down; occasional visits might be fine; she'll ask her landlord herself when ready.
2. *A: wants to plan weekend trips without negotiating every use; needs the trailer for those trips; sharing could work if scheduled around her weekends.
3. *A: worried that B would rather the trailer weren't there, and doesn't want that to leave her without it for her trips; doesn't yet know what comes next.

Which meet your needs? Which fail? Even a minor discomfort — I want it. "No" is welcome; it tells me what to add.

A and C mostly meet my needs. But a booking list needs a clear deadline for posting dates and a fair rule for actual overlaps; otherwise we’re back to negotiating. B can ask her landlord in parallel, but I can’t assume storage won’t affect access until we know what’s allowed. And I’m not ready to say B’s wish can’t affect whether I get to use the trailer.

Fair — and you're right, draft B as written doesn't meet your main wish; it only protects the dates. Let me add a fourth draft that goes at your actual concern, without anyone committing to anything:

D. A destination hunt, at your pace. Before your landlord question can lead anywhere, we need to know a move is even possible. So: does anyone know of a plausible spot — A's or C's own property, a yard, a lot, a rented space at one of your workplaces (A and C work together, so that's one lead to check)? That's homework and questions, not a decision, and it costs nobody any dates. If no destination exists, the landlord question changes shape — and you'd know that before spending goodwill with him.

So your wish stands on the list as its own item, not folded into the dates. Your call on the pace: I'm not going to ask you to chase a landlord or a destination before you're ready.

Also, and I want to be straight with you: A has told me she's worried that you'd rather the trailer weren't there, because she doesn't want to be left without it for her trips. I'm not asking you to resolve that — just making sure you heard it from me rather than through the fence. When you reply on the drafts, tell me if D helps, and any minor discomfort with anything.

D helps, especially if the destination search is something we all share rather than something I have to manage. A and C make sense for the dates. I do feel a little awkward about A worrying I’ll leave her without the trailer; I’m not trying to take away her trips, but I would like it moved off my pad.
